documents.text:
# Charter for Robotics Norway

**Status:** Draft · 6 November 2026 · For the steering group  
**Founding meeting:** 5 November 2026, Startuplab, Oslo

This charter sets out the purpose, membership, organisation and activities of the Robotics Norway business network. Where earlier invitations or presentations mention membership fees or a central network budget, the rules in this charter apply.

---

## § 1 Purpose

Robotics Norway is the business network for companies that build robots, physical AI, and the data and software around them. The network gives members a shared route to customers, partners, talent and investors in Norway and abroad.

The network shall be easy to join, complementary to other robotics networks and clusters, and run by its members.

---

## § 2 Membership

1. The network is open to all robotics companies in Norway.  
2. Individuals may also become members if they live in Norway, or work for a Norwegian robotics company or at a Norwegian university, university college or research institute.  
3. The network may open for international members by decision of the steering group.  
4. Membership is free. The network has no budget and charges no membership fee.  
5. A company becomes a member by joining the network’s email list and accepting that its logo, contact person and company information are published on the network’s website.  
6. An individual becomes a member in the same way and accepts that their name, and their affiliation if they give one, are published on the network’s website. Their contact details are not published.  
7. A member leaves by notifying the administrator. Withdrawal takes effect when the administrator has confirmed receipt, and the member’s information is removed from the website within a reasonable time.  
8. Membership in Robotics Norway does not preclude simultaneous membership in other networks or clusters.

---

## § 3 Organisation

1. The network is governed by a steering group composed of volunteers among the members.  
2. The steering group sets priorities, coordinates activities and adopts amendments to this charter.  
3. The network leader and the administration rotate and each term lasts one year.  
4. Leader for 2027 is Lars-Fredrik Forberg, CEO of Kinetic Blocks. Kinetic Blocks AS is the administrator company in 2027. The steering group appoints the leader and administrator for subsequent years.  
5. No member may bind the other members without a mandate from the steering group.

*At the founding meeting on 5 November 2026 the following were confirmed for the steering group: Daniel (Saro Robotics), Eva (Necia), Christian Rokseth (Humanoid.guide) and Runway FBU. Others may join by contacting the administrator.*

---

## § 4 Activities

1. **Network meetings.** The network shall arrange an unspecified number of network meetings each year.  
2. **Collaboration.** The network shall collaborate with other robotics networks and clusters in Norway and abroad.  
3. **Study trips.** The network shall arrange an unspecified number of study trips each year. These are financed by the members who take part.  
4. **Projects.** The network shall establish, seek funding for and carry out specific projects for relevant members. Such projects are financed by the member companies that take part, and where applicable by public grants. Participation is voluntary and creates no obligations for other members.  
5. **Robot labs.** The network shall support the establishment of robot labs in Norway, but shall not finance them. Labs have their own budgets and their own funding applications.

---

## § 5 Finances

1. Robotics Norway as a network is free to join and has no central budget.  
2. Costs of study trips are covered by the members who take part.  
3. Costs of specific projects are covered by the member companies that take part in the project, and where applicable by grants sought for that project.  
4. Robot labs are not financed by the network.

---

## § 6 Digital assets

1. The network owns the domain **roboticsnorway.org**.  
2. The website shall display member companies’ logos, contact persons and company information, and individual members’ names, in accordance with § 2.  
3. The administrator manages the domain and website on behalf of the network during their term of office, and hands over access to the next administrator.

---

## § 7 Trust between members

1. Market information shared in the network shall be treated as confidential unless the member who shares it states otherwise.  
2. Each member runs its own business freely, including with customers and partners contacted through the network.

---

## § 8 Amendments

Amendments to this charter are adopted by the steering group. Amendments to § 2 items 1–7 and § 5 (membership and a free network with no budget) require clear consent from the members, not only a simple majority of the steering group.

---

*Draft prepared 6 November 2026 based on the founding meeting presentation and the decisions on a free network, membership via email list, rotating leadership and administration, activities, robot labs, and the domain roboticsnorway.org.*

## A. Public charter (English original)

From the founding meeting slides, 5 November 2026, Startuplab, Oslo. Slide title: CHARTER / WHAT ROBOTICS NORWAY WILL BE.

Robotics Norway is the network/cluster for Norwegian companies that build robots, physical AI and the data and software around them, and gives its members a shared route to buyers, partners, talent and investors at home and abroad.

### Open membership
Open to robotics companies and organisations in Norway, and to individuals who live in Norway or work for a Norwegian robotics company or in academia.

### Run by its members
Members elect the steering group and take turns as administrator, one year at a time.

### 500 robot labs
Five (hundred) labs in Norwegian cities where members test, collect data and demonstrate, starting at Startuplab.

### Study trips
Joint trips to Odense, San Francisco and Shenzhen to meet clusters, buyers and manufacturers together.

### A door to the Bay Area
A funded project, led by Innovation Norway, that introduces Norwegian robotics companies to the Bay Area.

### Trust between members
Market information shared in the network stays confidential, and every member runs its own business freely.

Notes from the same deck (not part of the six charter bullets, but presented as the network's purpose and next decisions):
- Signing a letter of intent establishes the project for Innovation Norway; the binding cooperation agreement, including any cash contribution, comes later.
- Kinetic Blocks AS is proposed as rotating administrator for 2027.
- Company presentations and de minimis declarations are requested by 20 November 2026.
- Steering group confirmed at the meeting (Granola notes): Daniel (Saro Robotics), Eva (Necia), Christian Rokseth (Humanoid.guide) and Runway FBU. Others invited to join by email. The steering group was to land the charter and coordinate with existing clusters.

searchDocuments.title: Humanoids at work: Startuplab and IMD Alumni Club of Norway bring physical AI to Norwegian business
searchDocuments.text:
Startuplab and IMD Alumni Club of Norway gathered business leaders, startups and robots to explore what humanoids can do at work.

Events

Marie Mostad, CEO of Startuplab, opens Humanoids at work in front of a full house.

Photos: Startuplab

The 1990s gave us the PC, the 2000s the internet, then came the smartphone, and now AI. Will humanoids shape the 2030s and beyond?

On 5 November, Startuplab and the IMD Alumni Club of Norway hosted "Humanoids at work" for Startuplab's Corporate Innovation Network. The aim was to lower the threshold, take the edge off what can feel intimidating, and get people thinking about testing and using robots in their own businesses. The event brought together large companies, startups and scale-ups. Marie Mostad, CEO of Startuplab, opened the afternoon.

The money is moving in

Capital is pouring into the field. More funding has already been raised for humanoid robotics in 2026 than in 2024 and 2025 combined. According to Christian Rokseth, founder of Humanoid.guide, a new humanoid is launched roughly every day. Even so, most of the activity is still about research and showing up at events. But that is how every new technology starts.

Lars-Fredrik Forberg, IMD Alumni Club and Kinetic Blocks, presents the charter for Robotics Norway.

Christian Rokseth, Humanoid.guide, on the humanoid makers to know in China, the USA and Europe.

Photos: Startuplab

From observing to doing

Robotics is not new, and the industry is well under way. As Sigrid Kjønnø Schaanning of Cognite showed, robots are moving from observing, for example on inspection rounds on oil platforms, to carrying out tasks that until now have been reserved for people. Fine motor skills, the fingertip feel humans train from infancy, are being practised hard, and progress is fast.

Sigrid Kjønnø Schaanning, Cognite, on robotics and autonomous industry.

Photos: Startuplab

Will we be replaced?

In the panel, moderated by Christina Wiig of Startuplab, Marcus Horn (Dotspot) and Lone Werness Bekkeheien (Marselia Robotics) pointed out that many people in the field look forward to getting rid of boring tasks, and believe it will free up time for more important work. As with generative AI, the key is to let employees decide and become the experts on what should be automated, and how. Mandate, budget and ownership belong in the line organisation. In other words: good change management.

This matters to all of us. Half of the world economy is physical work, and sectors such as health, hospitality and mobility need more hands. Imagine a humanoid that cleans and tidies, so home care workers have time to sit down with the elderly. "People will now get more time for people," said Julian Alexander Hahn of Wybe.

From left: Sigrid Kjønnø Schaanning (Cognite), Marcus Horn (Dotspot), Lone Werness Bekkeheien (Marselia Robotics), Christian Rokseth (Humanoid.guide) and moderator Christina Wiig (Startuplab).

Photos: Startuplab

A late visitor from Moss

Julian Alexander Hahn, founder of Wybe Robotics in Moss, arrived at the very end with a humanoid in tow. Wybe builds what it calls robotic employees. It starts as software on a small on-premises device, the Wybe Node, which handles calls, emails, scheduling and follow-ups around the clock in more than 30 languages. When a role needs hands, the same "brain" can be given a humanoid body for cleaning, reception or security. Wybe buys the robot bodies from hardware partners and installs its own software, safety systems and intelligence at its R&D lab in Moss. Consumers can now reserve a Wybe for the home, guided at first through VR teleoperation, with deliveries to Norwegian homes planned before the new year.

Julian Alexander Hahn of Wybe Robotics (right) presents the Wybe, steered by a colleague wearing a VR headset.

A member of the Wybe team tries VR teleoperation of the humanoid.

Photos: Startuplab

Missed this time: Per Ivar Selvaag

Per Ivar Selvaag, former VP of Design at 1X Technologies, where he led the design of the NEO home humanoid, and a lead designer at BMW before that, was due to speak but was ill on the day. His planned talk argued that the uncanny valley is a business problem, not an aesthetic one: whether people accept a humanoid in their home or workplace comes down to design. We hope to hear him at a later event.

What should you do?

Those who start early gain a big advantage when the technology matures. Do you have tasks that are physical, repetitive, boring or unsafe? Map them. Collect data. Test. Robot Garden at Fornebu is a physical test arena for industry, and digital simulations take you a long way. Lars-Fredrik Forberg, who also presented the Robotics Norway network and its charter at the event, is building Kinetic Blocks, a marketplace for robot training data.

And at home? Many are waiting for their Neo from 1X, and you can now also rent one through Wybe in time for Christmas. Perhaps 2026 is the last year you sort your own laundry.

Bettina Lycke of Startuplab closed the afternoon, and the conversation continued over mingling with humans and humanoids alike.

Guests meet the humanoid after the talks.

Photos: Startuplab

Thanks to everyone who took part, and especially to Christian Rokseth (Humanoid.guide), Sigrid Kjønnø Schaanning (Cognite), Lars-Fredrik Forberg (Kinetic Blocks), Marcus Horn (Dotspot), Lone Werness Bekkeheien (Marselia Robotics), Julian Alexander Hahn (Wybe Robotics), and the driving force Christina Wiig (Startuplab).

searchDocuments.title: Robotics Norway is founded
searchDocuments.text:
Participants met in person and online at StartupLab in Oslo on 5 November 2026 for the founding meeting of the Robotics Norway network.

Network

Participants at the founding meeting.

Photos: StartupLab

On 5 November 2026, Robotics Norway held its founding meeting at StartupLab in Oslo. Participants joined in person and online. The public charter from the meeting describes Robotics Norway as the network and cluster for Norwegian companies that build robots, physical AI, and the data and software around them.

The charter states the purpose of the network. It is to give members a shared route to buyers, partners, talent and investors, at home and abroad. It is written for companies and organisations in robotics and physical AI, and it is also open to individuals who join as private members. The wording is the English text from the founding-meeting slides, whose title is CHARTER / WHAT ROBOTICS NORWAY WILL BE. That text is published on this site.

The charter has six points.

Open membership. The network is open to companies and organisations in robotics and physical AI, and to individuals as private members.

Run by its members. Members elect the steering group and take turns as administrator, one year at a time.

Five hundred robot labs. The charter calls for labs in Norwegian cities where members test, collect data and demonstrate, starting at StartupLab. The heading on the slide is 500 robot labs.

Study trips. Members are to make joint trips to Odense, San Francisco and Shenzhen to meet clusters, buyers and manufacturers together.

A door to the Bay Area. The charter describes a funded project, led by Innovation Norway, that introduces Norwegian robotics companies to the Bay Area.

Trust between members. Market information shared in the network stays confidential, and every member runs its own business freely.

Lars-Fredrik Forberg, who chaired the founding meeting, presents next steps for Robotics Norway to participants in the room and online.

Exchanging ideas beside the staircase.

Outside StartupLab Hardware.

Lars-Fredrik Forberg chaired the founding meeting of Robotics Norway.

Photos: StartupLab

Taken together, the points describe a network run by its members. They elect the steering group and take turns as administrator, one year at a time. They share a route to buyers, partners, talent and investors in Norway and abroad. Market information shared among them stays confidential, and each member runs its own business freely. The practical work named in the charter is robot labs in Norwegian cities, starting at StartupLab, joint study trips to Odense, San Francisco and Shenzhen, and a funded Bay Area project led by Innovation Norway. The same six headings are published on the front page of this site.

What the meeting agreed

Around 30 companies and organisations took part, in the room and online, from startups to Ruter, Posten Bring, Cognite and Oslo kommune. The participants backed the initiative and agreed on three things.

A small steering group was formed, with Daniel Kjøle Skogland (Saro Robotics), Eva (Necia), Christian Rokseth (Humanoid.guide) and Runway FBU confirmed, and others invited to join. Four to five companies signed up their interest in "A door to the Bay Area", and a letter of intent is now going out so the network can apply to Innovation Norway. Around 16 people raised their hands for a study trip to Shenzhen, which will be coordinated with the Norwegian Robotics Cluster.

Robotics Norway is meant to complement existing networks such as the Norwegian Robotics Cluster and Necia, not compete with them, and members are free to take part in several. Before any new labs are built, the network will map the robot labs and test arenas that already exist across Norway.

Read the full minutes of the founding meeting.

The agenda of the founding meeting covered adopting the charter, the "A door to the Bay Area" project, administration, the budget and a steering group. Participants were there in person at StartupLab and online.

Companies, organisations and individuals who want to take part can find out how to join on the Join page. The projects anchored in the network, including "A door to the Bay Area", are described on the Projects page.

Read Shifter's coverage of the founding meeting (in Norwegian): Starter nytt robotikk-nettverk

searchDocuments.title: Kristoffer Gjerde
searchDocuments.text: Kristoffer Gjerde. Director, Strategic Accounts, Cognite. Director of Strategic Accounts at Cognite, where he drives commercial growth with leading oil and gas operators while continuing to champion the use of robotics in industrial operations. He joined Cognite in 2021 and spent 2022 to 2025 in Riyadh as Head of Robotics at CNTXT, Cognite's joint venture with Aramco. He then returned to shape Cognite's robotics strategy as Director of Robotics Strategy, focusing on bringing autonomous inspection into day-to-day operations. MSc in Computer Science, specialising in Artificial Intelligence.

searchDocuments.title: Lito
searchDocuments.text: Lito. Robotics data lab in Oslo that collects manipulation training data with wireless handheld grippers (stereo video, motion, gripper opening, and planned fingertip touch). Founded by Thomas Sørensen (CEO) and Ludvig Øvrevik (CTO).. Thomas Soerensen. thomas@lito.so. https://lito.so

searchDocuments.title: Marselia Robotics
searchDocuments.text: Marselia Robotics. Industrial robots, based in Stavanger (as introduced by Lone). Press coverage describes software that lets an operator instruct a robot arm in ordinary language.. Lone. lone@marseliarobotics.com

searchDocuments.title: Mechatronics Innovation Lab
searchDocuments.text: Mechatronics Innovation Lab. Lab in Grimstad working with robotics, AI and additive manufacturing. Invitation notes equipment including Unitree G1, a quadruped, and Boston Dynamics Spot.. Jayant Singh. Jayant@mil-as.no

searchDocuments.title: Necia
searchDocuments.text: Necia. Necia Tech Cluster works on Industry 4.0, automation, AI and humanoid robotics in the Moss region, with about 23 member companies. Part of EU project eViva and planning an international Robotics Expo in Moss.. Eva Helen Rognskog. er@necia.no. https://necia.no

searchDocuments.title: Norwegian Robotics Cluster
searchDocuments.text: Norwegian Robotics Cluster. Industry cluster funded by Innovation Norway, based on Osterøy, bringing together producers, integrators, end users, research, capital and public actors. Admitted to NIC Connect for 2027–2029 according to the founding slides.. Vidar Tufteland. vidar@robotcluster.no

searchDocuments.title: Oslo kommune, Sykehjemsetaten
searchDocuments.text: Oslo kommune, Sykehjemsetaten. Oslo’s nursing-home agency; introduced interest in nursing-home applications of robotics.. Johnny Advocaat. johnny.advocaat@sye.oslo.kommune.no. https://www.oslo.kommune.no/

searchDocuments.title: Physical Robotics
searchDocuments.text: Physical Robotics. Norwegian advanced robotics and automation company (Necia member page).. https://www.physicalrobotics.com

searchDocuments.title: Posten Bring
searchDocuments.text: Posten Bring. Interested in robotics and automation (as introduced by Camilla).. Camilla De Verdier. camilla.de.verdier@bring.com. https://www.bring.com

searchDocuments.title: PPM Robotics
searchDocuments.text: PPM Robotics. High-tech robot installations; now robots for nursing homes, based in Trondheim. Mentioned their Nursing Home Lab (NHL) in Trondheim during the meeting.. Trygve Thomessen. trygve.thomessen@ppm.no

searchDocuments.title: ROBOXI
searchDocuments.text: ROBOXI. About 30 employees in Stavanger; builds robots for airport aprons / autonomous runway inspection and maintenance (meeting intro and 3LC partnership page).. Magnus Olsen Finnesand. magnus@roboxi.com

searchDocuments.title: Runway FBU
searchDocuments.text: Runway FBU. Investment fund for the future of industry including robotics; also runs an AI/robotics hub (as introduced by Hanna Selvaag Wangsmo and Maria Katarina Michelsen). LinkedIn company page describes a tech hub with 60+ companies and an AI and Robotics Lab at Aker Tech House, Fornebu, related to RunwayVC (runway.vc).. Hanna Selvaag Wangsmo. hanna@runwayfbu.com

searchDocuments.title: Ruter AS
searchDocuments.text: Ruter AS. Researching the impact of robotics on public transport (as introduced by Vibeke Harlem).. Vibeke Harlem. vibeke.harlem@ruter.no. https://ruter.no

searchDocuments.title: Saro Robotics
searchDocuments.text: Saro Robotics. Builds autonomous climbing robots for inspection of industrial pipe networks, delivering continuous inspection data for energy infrastructure (including corrosion under insulation).. Ingeborg Sofie Bogen. ingeborg@sarorobotics.com. https://www.sarorobotics.com

searchDocuments.title: Sonair
searchDocuments.text: Sonair. Makes ADAR One, a safety-certified 3D ultrasonic sensor (SIL 2 / PL d) for detecting people and obstacles around robots.. Tor Odland. tor@sonair.com. https://sonair.com

searchDocuments.title: Startuplab
searchDocuments.text: Startuplab. Norway’s largest tech incubator, with a hardware, deep tech and defence focus (as introduced at the founding meeting). Host of the founding meeting and the agreed first robot lab in Oslo.. Kristian Hesthaug. kristian@startuplab.no. https://www.startuplab.no

searchDocuments.title: Takt Logistikk
searchDocuments.text: Takt Logistikk. Helps contractors and developers take control of construction-site logistics: planning, coordinated deliveries and digital information sharing from planning to completed project, based on Lean Construction.. Gjermund Lien. gjermund@taktlogistikk.no. https://taktlogistikk.no

searchDocuments.title: Wybe Robotics
searchDocuments.text: Wybe Robotics. Builds robotic employees from its R&D lab in Moss. The Wybe Node, a small on-premises device, handles calls, emails, scheduling and follow-ups around the clock in more than 30 languages, and the same software can be given a humanoid body for cleaning, reception or security.. Julian Alexander Hahn. julian@wybe.me. https://wybe.me
